## Isaiah 27 — Verse-by-Verse Notes

### v. 1: “In that day the LORD will take His sharp, great, and mighty sword, and bring judgment on Leviathan the fleeing serpent—Leviathan the coiling serpent—and He will slay the dragon of the sea.”

**Traditional Reading**

The “day” is the final triumph of the Messiah’s kingdom, continuing the eschatological theme of Isaiah 24–27. The “sword” of the Lord — described as sore (or keen), great, and strong — is the instrument of this decisive judgment. Leviathan is understood as a monstrous, serpentine foe connected with the sea, resisting God, whose destiny is destruction at the Lord’s hand. Many commentators connect Leviathan to Satan, noting that Revelation uses similar dragon/serpent imagery for the devil (Rev 12:9; 20:2). David Guzik argues that while some treat the language as mythological illustration, Isaiah may be “more literal than many would like to admit” — if Satan appeared as a serpent in Eden, he could manifest as a sea-dragon.
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-27/

Gill sees the sword as either the Word of God (the sword of the Spirit) or the great power of God’s judicial sentence, and identifies Leviathan as earthly powers opposed to the church — culminating in Rome (both pagan and papal), the Turk, and Satan himself.
— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/isaiah/27.htm

Ellicott interprets the threefold description (fleeing serpent, crooked serpent, dragon in the sea) as pointing to three great world-powers: Assyria (the rapid Tigris), Babylon (the winding Euphrates), and Egypt (the Nile and sea). Others (Cheyne) see the three as symbols of rebel powers of evil and darkness, not earthly empires. The Pulpit Commentary likewise sees a “triple judgment on the powers of darkness,” identifying the three figures with “the devil, the beast, and the false prophet” of Revelation.
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/isaiah-27.html
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/isaiah-27.html

**Baptist (Gill):** Identifies Leviathan mystically as earthly rulers and antichristian powers — Rome pagan and papal, the Turk, and Satan at the head of all. The “sword” is either the Word of God or judgment executed through human instruments (e.g., Medes and Persians against Babylon).
— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/isaiah/27.htm

**Methodist (Whedon):** Sees three representative world-powers: Assyria (the fleeing serpent on the rapid Tigris), Babylon (the crooked serpent on the winding Euphrates), and Egypt (the dragon of the Nile). All three had harassed Israel and all would be judged.
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/whe/isaiah-27.html

**Catholic (Haydock/Challoner):** Identifies Leviathan as “the devil, the great enemy of the people of God … spiritually slain by the death of Christ, when his power was destroyed.” It may also refer literally to Nebuchadnezzar or the king of Egypt.
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/hcc/isaiah-27.html

**Scholarship (Constable, via StudyLight):** Notes that Leviathan appears in Ugaritic mythology (Lotan, the chaos monster destroyed by Baal). Isaiah’s use does not imply belief in the myth; he uses it as illustration. Constable favours the view that Leviathan stands for the strong spiritual enemies of God’s people, probably Satan himself.
— Excerpt from Constable’s Notes via StudyLight search results

---

### v. 2: “In that day: ‘Sing about a fruitful vineyard.’”

**Traditional Reading**

This verse opens a “song of the vineyard” that deliberately reverses the dirge of Isaiah 5:1–7. There the vineyard (Israel) was unfruitful and given over to desolation; here it is fruitful (“red wine” or “foaming wine”) and is to be sung about. Ellicott notes that the prophet who chanted a dirge over the unfruitful vineyard now “changes the wailing into a poem.” The Pulpit Commentary says the vineyard here is “either the Christian Church, or the Jewish Church reformed and purified by suffering.”
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/isaiah-27.html
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/isaiah-27.html
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-27/

**Catholic (Haydock):** The vineyard is “the Church of Christ.”
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/hcc/isaiah-27.html

---

### v. 3: “I, the LORD, am its keeper; I water it continually. I guard it night and day so no one can disturb it.”

**Traditional Reading**

Every word reverses the judgment pronounced in Isaiah 5. Instead of abandonment, there is constant care; instead of drought, continual watering; instead of being overrun by spoilers, Jehovah Himself keeps it night and day. Gill notes that the watering is “both more immediately with the dews of his grace … and more immediately by the ministry of the word and ordinances.” Guzik emphasises God’s active, personal, unceasing care.
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/isaiah-27.html
— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/isaiah/27.htm
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-27/

**Matthew Henry:** “We need the continual waterings of Divine grace; if these be at any time withdrawn, we wither, and come to nothing.”
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/mhn/isaiah-27.html

---

### v. 4: “I am not angry. If only thorns and briers confronted Me, I would march and trample them, I would burn them to the ground.”

**Traditional Reading**

“Fury is not in me” — Ellicott renders it “There is no wrath in me.” God’s anger against His vineyard has passed. But if “briars and thorns” (symbols of the enemies of His people, as in Isa 9:18; 10:17; 2 Sam 23:6–7) should arise against Him, He will do battle against them and consume them utterly. The Pulpit Commentary sees the briars and thorns as “unrighteous members of the Church” or enemies who dare to oppose Him. Guzik sees this as God’s promise to deal with anything that threatens His vineyard.
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/isaiah-27.html
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/isaiah-27.html
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-27/

**Gill:** The fury is not against His vineyard; there is no wrath in His heart towards His people, though they may deserve it. The thorns and briars are hypocrites and false teachers within the visible church whom God will consume.
— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/isaiah/27.htm

---

### v. 5: “Or let them lay claim to My protection; let them make peace with Me—yes, let them make peace with Me.”

**Traditional Reading**

This is a strikingly evangelical invitation. Even the enemies (“thorns and briars”) have an alternative: they may “take hold of My strength” (lit. “lay hold of My fortress”) and make peace with God. Ellicott says the thought is that “even the enemies of Jehovah, if repentant, may find in Him their castle and deliverer.” Guzik (citing Poole) connects “take hold of My strength” to Jacob wrestling with the angel — strength received from God, not one’s own. The doubled phrase “make peace with Me” underscores the earnestness of the invitation. The Pulpit Commentary calls it “a truly evangelical invitation! The enemies of God are entreated to cease from striving against him.”
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/isaiah-27.html
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-27/
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/isaiah-27.html

**Gill:** “Take hold of my strength” means lay hold of Christ, “who is the strength and power of God … a strong tower … to whom saints may betake themselves, and be safe.” Peace is not made by the believer’s own efforts but by Christ, “the only peacemaker.”
— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/isaiah/27.htm

**Matthew Henry:** “Pardoning mercy is called the power of our Lord; let us take hold on that. Christ crucified is the power of God.”
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/mhn/isaiah-27.html

---

### v. 6: “In the days to come, Jacob will take root. Israel will bud and blossom and fill the whole world with fruit.”

**Traditional Reading**

Ellicott renders, “In the days that come Jacob shall strike root.” The figure shifts from vineyard to a single vine. The true Israel shall go through normal stages of growth and its restoration shall bless the whole world — “the riches of the Gentiles” (Rom 11:12). Guzik sees ultimate fulfilment in the Millennial Kingdom but applies it now: “if we yield to the care of the LORD, He will care for us as His precious vineyard right now.” Constable (via excerpts) notes that amillennialists see a spiritual fulfilment in the progress of the gospel, while premillennialists look for a literal future regathering and flourishing of national Israel.
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/isaiah-27.html
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-27/

---

### v. 7: “Has the LORD struck Israel as He struck her oppressors? Was she killed like those who slayed her?”

**Traditional Reading**

The implied answer is “No.” God has disciplined Israel but not with the severity He used against Israel’s oppressors. Ellicott explains: “Jehovah had chastised the guilt with a leniency altogether exceptional. They had not been punished as others had been.” An alternative reading preferred by some: Jehovah did not smite Israel with the kind of smiting with which Israel’s smiters smote — i.e., not ruthlessly and in hate, but in mercy. Constable: God “had always demonstrated special care and restraint when He dealt with His chosen people.”
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/isaiah-27.html
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-27/

---

### v. 8: “By warfare and exile You contended with her and removed her with a fierce wind, as on the day the east wind blows.”

**Traditional Reading**

Ellicott gives the literal sense: “with measure and measure” — the word for “measure” is the *seah* (a third of an ephah), proverbially small, expressing extreme moderation in God’s chastisements. The “sending away” alludes to divorce (Hosea 1–3), but God did not carry the proceedings to the full rigour of the law. The “rough wind” / “east wind” imagery: Ellicott argues that “stay” (or “remove”) means “sifting” rather than restraining — God sifts with the rough wind; punishment is reformatory, not merely penal. The Pulpit Commentary: “Amid the rough and stern severity … there was an undertone of sadness and grief.”
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/isaiah-27.html
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/isaiah-27.html

**Catholic (Haydock/Challoner):** “When the synagogue shall be cast off, thou shalt judge it in measure, and in proportion to its crimes.”
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/hcc/isaiah-27.html

---

### v. 9: “Therefore Jacob’s guilt will be atoned for, and the full fruit of the removal of his sin will be this: When he makes all the altar stones like crushed bits of chalk, no Asherah poles or incense altars will remain standing.”

**Traditional Reading**

The chastisement of v. 8 is the instrument of purification. “By this” — the measured punishment — Jacob’s iniquity is purged. The “fruit” of taking away sin will be the total destruction of idolatrous worship: altar stones ground to chalk, Asherah poles and incense altars demolished. Ellicott notes the LXX rendering (“when I shall take away their sins”) is quoted by Paul in Romans 11:27. Guzik: “The LORD shows His mercy to Israel in that He destroys their idolatrous altars and images, forcing them to worship the LORD only.” The Pulpit Commentary sees this spirit strongly manifested in the Maccabean period.
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/isaiah-27.html
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-27/
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/isaiah-27.html

**Gill:** Afflictions are not themselves atonements for sin; they are means of bringing God’s people to repentance and confession. The true atonement comes from Christ.
— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/isaiah/27.htm

**Matthew Henry:** “The design of affliction is to part between them and sin. The affliction has done us good, when we keep at a distance from the occasions of sin.”
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/mhn/isaiah-27.html

---

### vv. 10–11: “For the fortified city lies deserted … For this is a people without understanding. Therefore their Maker has no compassion on them, and their Creator shows them no favor.”

**Traditional Reading**

Ellicott: the “defenced city” is the city of Israel’s enemies (cf. Isaiah 25:2), not Jerusalem. Its desolation is total — calves graze where streets once bustled; women gather withered branches for firewood. The people are “without understanding” — they did not discern their need to submit to God. Therefore their Maker shows them no favour. Guzik identifies this as “the city of man, representing the world system.” The Pulpit Commentary, however, takes the city as Jerusalem itself — “though her punishment is in mercy … yet Jerusalem shall for a time be desolate.”
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/isaiah-27.html
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-27/
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/isaiah-27.html

**Catholic (Haydock):** Identifies the city as Jerusalem (or possibly Babylon).
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/hcc/isaiah-27.html

---

### v. 12: “In that day the LORD will thresh from the flowing Euphrates to the Wadi of Egypt, and you, O Israelites, will be gathered one by one.”

**Traditional Reading**

The verb “thresh” (or “beat off”) is the same used for beating out grain or olives (Isa 28:27; Deut 24:20). It pictures an abundant harvest-gathering, yet “one by one” — each individual receives undivided care. The boundaries “from the Euphrates to the Wadi of Egypt” represent the full ideal extent of the Promised Land (Gen 15:18; 1 Kgs 8:65). Ellicott: “Judah and Israel should once more be peopled as in the days of old.” The Pulpit Commentary: “The Israel of God gathered in and garnered one by one … salvation is an individual matter.”
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/isaiah-27.html
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/isaiah-27.html
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-27/

---

### v. 13: “And in that day a great ram’s horn will sound, and those who were perishing in Assyria will come forth with those who were exiles in Egypt. And they will worship the LORD on the holy mountain in Jerusalem.”

**Traditional Reading**

The “great trumpet” recalls the silver trumpets of Numbers 10 for assembling the camp, and especially the Jubilee trumpet of Leviticus 25:9 — the proclamation of the Year of Redemption. It reappears in the eschatology of Matt 24:31, 1 Cor 15:52, and 1 Thess 4:16. Assyria and Egypt represent the nations among whom Israel was scattered. The gathering culminates in worship on the holy mountain in Jerusalem. Ellicott: “That purpose … is the proclamation of the Year of Redemption, the restoration of the dispersed of Israel.” Constable (via excerpts): amillennialists interpret this as the conversion of Gentiles to Christ; premillennialists see a literal regathering of Israel.
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/isaiah-27.html
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-27/

**Catholic (Challoner):** “The great trumpet — the preaching of the Gospel for the conversion of the Jews.”
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/hcc/isaiah-27.html

**Spurgeon (Baptist):** Preached on “ready to perish” from this verse for those under conviction of sin: “This is the way in which God begins with those whom he intends to bless … He destroys our confidence in our own works, and then gives us confidence in Christ’s work.”
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/spe/isaiah-27.html

## Summary of Key Interpretative Differences

| Issue | View |
|-------|------|
| **Leviathan (v. 1)** | **Historic Protestant (Ellicott, Whedon):** Assyria, Babylon, Egypt as world-powers. **Pulpit/Catholic/Guzik:** Satan and spiritual powers of darkness. **Gill:** Antichristian powers (Rome, Turk) with Satan at their head. |
| **The vineyard (vv. 2–6)** | **Most Protestants:** Israel restored, ultimately in the Millennial Kingdom, with a present spiritual application to the Church. **Catholic (Haydock/Challoner):** Explicitly “the Church of Christ.” **Amillennialists:** Spiritual fulfilment in the gospel’s spread. **Premillennialists:** Literal future regathering of national Israel. |
| **The “defenced city” (vv. 10–11)** | **Ellicott/Guzik:** The world-system / city of Israel’s enemies. **Pulpit Commentary:** Jerusalem itself, desolate for a time. |
| **The trumpet and regathering (vv. 12–13)** | **Premillennial/Dispensational:** Literal end-time regathering of Israel. **Amillennial/Reformed:** The ingathering of elect Jews and Gentiles into the Church through the gospel. **Catholic (Challoner):** The preaching of the Gospel for the conversion of the Jews. **Spurgeon:** Applied evangelistically to the salvation of individual sinners “ready to perish.” |
